Subject: Post-call: performance coverage & token capacity playbook for Acme Analytics

Hi Sanjay / Priya —

Thanks again for taking the time today. Short recap + proposed next steps so we have shared expectations before the technical deep-dive: 

1) High-level SLA targets you called out
   - Interactive UI latency: P95 <= 150 ms for single-turn generation (most requests are single-turn retrieval + generation)
   - Streaming: low-latency partial token delivery for transcript/assist flow (need incremental tokens within ~100ms once generation starts)
   - Concurrency goal: baseline 200 concurrent active sessions, burst to 500 for periodic spikes

2) Token/context profile (ballpark from today)
   - Typical input: 4k–8k tokens (most sessions)
   - Heavy inputs: up to ~12k tokens when including long log history/snippets (rare, ~5% of requests)
   - Output: usually 200–800 tokens; occasionally up to 2k for detailed summaries
   - Monthly token estimate you mentioned: ~250M tokens (mixed compressions)

3) Operational concerns we should cover in the follow-up call
   - Preferred routing: US-only region; data residency for logs handled per agreement
   - Fallbacks: what model variants to use when capacity constrained (latency vs. cost tradeoff)
   - Observability: per-route latency, queueing, and P95 tracking (we can expose dashboards and alerting)

Next steps I propose:
   - Schedule a 60–90 minute technical qualification with Marissa (SE) + your SRE/infra folks to run through a targeted perf matrix and sample prompts
   - You to share a representative prompt set + 2–3 example heavy records (sanitized) for perf-sim
   - Redwood will produce an initial throughput/latency matrix and proposed deployment topology (dedicated vs. hosted)

I attached brief discovery notes and our proposed throughput matrix template for the call (see attachments). Please confirm the SLA targets above are accurate or flag anything I misunderstood.

Thanks,
Jordan Blake
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
[jordan.blake@redwood.com]

Jordan —

Thanks for the clear recap. A few clarifications from our side: 

- Latency: 150 ms P95 is the target for short single-turn queries (yes). For multi-turn UI flows where we stream progressively, we care much more about time-to-first-byte and incremental token latency (we typically need partial tokens to appear in the client within ~100ms of generation start).
- Concurrency: 200 concurrent *active* sessions is the baseline. Note that our usage pattern has many idle websockets; active sessions translate roughly to 60–70% of connected users at peak. We expect periodic spikes during end-of-day reporting where concurrency can jump to 450–500 for 2–10 minute windows.
- Context: most requests are 6k tokens or below, but we do sometimes send bundles of logs that reach ~12k. Those heavy cases are important but can be relegated to an async path if they materially impact latency for the interactive flow.

Two questions for Redwood: 
1) How would you recommend handling the 12k cases without compromising P95 for interactive sessions? (Is prefix/KV caching adequate, or do we need a separate model topology?)
2) What are rough cost implications of running dedicated capacity that meets our target (order-of-magnitude is fine at this stage)?

We can do the technical deep-dive next week — Priya (cc) will coordinate availability. Please include Marissa and relevant perf engineers.

Best,
Sanjay
CTO, Acme Analytics

Hi Sanjay —

Thanks, this is helpful. A few technical notes / concrete suggestions ahead of the perf session: 

1) Handling heavy (12k) inputs without regressing interactive P95
   - Option A (preferred for predictability): Route heavy inputs to a separate async ingestion topology. Keep interactive paths on a lower context ceiling (8k) with prefix/KV caching enabled for repeated prompts.
   - Option B (if you need single topology): Use query-splitting + streaming reassembly; this reduces per-request peak memory but increases orchestration complexity.

2) Streaming behavior and time-to-first-byte
   - Streaming adds overhead on the runtime for token flushes; we typically see ~10–40 ms additional per-token emission cost depending on hardware and model variant. To hit ~100 ms time-to-first-byte in production, we recommend tuning batch windows aggressively (sub-30ms batching) and using smaller micro-batches for streaming endpoints.

3) Concurrency and fracture tests we recommend for qualification
   - Baseline test: 200 concurrent streaming sessions, 8k context, median output 400 tokens; run for 30 min to measure steady-state P95/99
   - Spike test: 500 concurrent non-streaming sessions (shorter outputs), 1–5 minute windows to measure queueing/backpressure behavior
   - Heavy-input test: 50 concurrent sessions with 12k contexts in async topology to instrument memory pressure and throughput

4) Deployment topology and cost guidance
   - For your profile, Dedicated capacity (reserved pools) gives predictable latency; a mixed strategy (hosted for low-volume async + dedicated for interactive) often hits both cost and latency targets. We'll quantify this in the throughput-matrix.xlsx attached.

What we need from you prior to the deep-dive:
   - Representative prompt set (10–20 prompts across categories: short query, long-log summarize, multi-turn assist)
   - A sanitized heavy record (one example of a 12k input) so we can reproduce memory profile
   - Availability window for next week (2-hour block preferably)

I've attached a filled example of the throughput matrix (throughput-matrix.xlsx) and a short checklist. Rishi, feel free to add anything on observability/alert thresholds.

Thanks,
Marissa Cole
